AHV Integrated Management Capabilities

  • You can manage the Nutanix platform from a single pane of glass with Nutanix Prism. Prism provides integrated capabilities for cluster management and VM management available from the Prism web console, command line interface (CLI), PowerShell, and REST API.

    Prism Central

    Prism Central is a centralized management solution that allows IT administrators to manage multiple Nutanix clusters from a single interface. It provides a unified control plane for monitoring, automation, analytics, and orchestration of virtualized and cloud environments.

    Prism Central key features

    • Single Pane of Glass Management – Enables administrators to manage multiple Nutanix clusters from one dashboard.
    • VM and Infrastructure Management – Facilitates provisioning, monitoring, and lifecycle management of virtual machines (VMs).
    • Capacity Planning & Analytics – Uses AI/ML-driven insights for capacity forecasting and workload optimization.
    • Security & Compliance – Includes security policies, anomaly detection, and compliance reporting.
    • Multi-Cloud Management – Integrates with public clouds (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) for hybrid cloud deployments.
    • Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) – Ensures security and governance by allowing specific user roles and permissions.

    Prism Central is a key component of Nutanix’s hyper-converged and disaggregated storage infrastructure ecosystem, making IT operations more efficient and scalable. It differs from Prism Element, which provides management at the cluster level, whereas Prism Central extends visibility and control across multiple clusters.

    Prism Central provides a streamlined way to manage virtual machines (VMs) and infrastructure across multiple Nutanix clusters. It simplifies IT operations by offering an intuitive, centralized interface for provisioning, monitoring, and scaling workloads.

    Figure 7.        The Prism Central Infrastructure Dashboard

    Prism Central benefits

    • Simplified Management – One interface for managing VMs across multiple clusters.
    • Operational Efficiency – Reduces manual workload with automation and AI-driven insights.
    • Scalability – Seamlessly scale VM resources without downtime.
    • Resilience – Built-in disaster recovery and high availability ensure uptime.

    APIs

    The Prism Central and Prism Element HTML5 interfaces are key components of Nutanix Cloud Platform (NCP) management. However, multiple use cases require programmatic control of Prism Central features and functions, combined with equivalent programmatic control over Nutanix products that integrate with Prism Central. Most functionality exposed through the Prism Central and Prism Element interfaces are also exposed through a full set of REST APIs. These APIs provide the ability to programmatically interface with the Nutanix platform, allowing customers and partners to enable automation, 3rd-party tools, scripts, apps or even create a customized UI if required.

    The Prism Central REST API exposes nearly every capability and data point of the Prism Central UI and allows for orchestration or automation tools to easily drive Nutanix actions. This enables tools like Terraform, Ansible, Saltstack, Puppet, Ansible and more to easily create custom workflows for Nutanix. Also, this means that any third-party developer could create their own custom UI and pull in Nutanix data via REST. Nutanix v4 APIs are the recommended version to be used for all use cases. All Nutanix v4 API documentation including SDK and API references is available at https://developers.nutanix.com.

    Cluster management

    Managing clusters on AHV involves creating, updating, deleting, and monitoring cluster resources. These resources include hosts, storage, and networks.

    Host profiles

    Prism provides a central location for administrators to update host settings like virtual networking and high availability across all nodes in an AHV cluster. Controlling configuration at the cluster level eliminates the need for manual compliance checks and reduces the risk of having a cluster that is not uniformly configured.

    Virtual networking

    AHV uses Open vSwitch (OVS) for all VM networking. When you create a new AHV cluster, the system configures the CVM and management networking paths automatically. Administrators can easily create new VLAN-backed layer 2 networks through Prism. After the administrator creates a network, they can assign it to existing and new VMs.

    Figure 8.        AHV VM Networking – Basic VLANs and Tags

    For more information on the AHV implementation of OVS, see the AHV Administration Guide.

    Along with streamlining VM network creation, AHV can manage DHCP addresses for each network that administrators create. This functionality allows administrators to configure address pools for each network that they can automatically assign to VMs.

    Nutanix Flow networking products offer advanced networking capabilities on AHV clusters. Nutanix Flow Virtual Networking brings virtual private cloud, virtual public cloud, and other advanced virtual networking constructs together to bridge traditional and cloud-native network models. With Nutanix Flow Network Security, you can create Zero Trust firewalls to segment and protect your users, apps, and data from cyber threats without disrupting your current infrastructure.

    For more information on AHV networking, see the AHV Networking best practice guide.

    Rolling upgrades

    Nutanix delivers a one-click upgrade process through Life Cycle Manager (LCM) for all software in the Nutanix platform, including AOS, AHV, firmware, and Nutanix Cluster Check (NCC). Upgrades are nondisruptive and allow the cluster to run continuously during software maintenance while nodes upgrade on a rolling basis in the background. LCM manages the dependencies between products and versions and only shows the supported upgrade options for your environment.

    Host maintenance mode

    Administrators can place AHV hosts in maintenance mode during upgrades and maintenance-related operations. Maintenance mode live-migrates all VMs running on the node to other nodes in the AHV cluster, and the CVM can safely shut down if required. After the maintenance process finishes all the steps for the node, it returns the CVM to service and synchronizes with other CVMs in the cluster. Maintenance mode enables graceful host suspension for routine cluster maintenance.

    VM operations

    Prism displays a list of all VMs in an AHV cluster along with configuration, resource usage, and performance details on a per-VM basis. Administrators can create VMs and perform many operations on selected VMs, including power state change, reset, shut down, restart, snapshot, and clone, migrate, category assignment, policy assignment, and launch a remote console. You can manage the entire life cycle of a VM and its policies that govern security and data protection from Prism.

    Image management

    The image management service in AHV is a centralized repository that provides access to virtual media and disk images and the ability to import from external sources. With AHV's image management service, you can store VMs or virtual disks as images, which you can then use to create new VMs quickly from a known-good base image. The image management service can store the virtual disk files you used to create the VMs or OS installation media as an .iso file that you can mount to provide a fresh OS install experience. Incorporated into Prism, the image management service can import and convert existing virtual disk formats, including .raw, .vhd, .vmdk, .vdi, and .qcow2. The previous virtual hardware settings do not constrain an imported virtual disk, so administrators have the flexibility to fully configure CPU, memory, virtual disks, and network settings when they provision VMs.

    OVA Import and Export

    Industry-standard Open Virtual Appliance (OVA) files are useful in many situations, but the most common are when you deploy virtual appliances (typically from a non-Nutanix vendor) and when you move VMs to a different hypervisor. To help you accomplish these tasks, the OVA import-and-export process is available in Prism Central. You can export VMs on AHV to the OVA format to keep them on external storage or import standard OVAs to launch third-party VMs quickly.

    VM templates

    The AHV image library captures data in a single vDisk so that you can clone it easily, requiring input from the administrator to declare the CPU, memory, and network details. VM templates simplify this concept further. You can create AHV VM templates from existing VMs, so that they inherit the attributes of the defining VM, such as the CPU, memory, and networking details. You can then configure the template to customize the guest OS on deployment and provide a Windows license key if needed for a Windows template.

    Figure 9.        Create Template from VM workflow

    VM templates support maintenance of multiple versions of a template, making it easy to apply updates like operating system and application patches without creating new templates. With the template versioning function, you can declare which version of the template is active, so that you can roll back to a previous version if needed or stage updates before making them available.

    Acropolis Dynamic Scheduler

    The Acropolis Dynamic Scheduler (ADS) is an automatic function enabled on every AHV cluster to avoid hot spots in cluster nodes. ADS continually monitors CPU, memory, and storage data points to make migration and initial placement decisions for VMs and Nutanix Volumes. Starting with existing statistical data for the cluster, ADS watches for anomalies, honors affinity controls, and only makes move decisions to avoid hot spots. Using machine learning, ADS can adjust move thresholds over time from their initial fixed values to achieve the greatest efficiency without sacrificing performance.

    ADS tracks each node's CPU and memory usage. When a node's CPU allocation breaches its threshold (currently 85 percent), Nutanix migrates VMs or Nutanix Volumes off that host as needed to rebalance the workload.

    ADS only uses migration when the system experiences contention. If the nodes experience skewed usage (for example, three nodes at 10 percent and one at 50 percent), ADS does not migrate the nodes, because migration offers minimal benefit if the system has enough resources.

    The following diagrams depict a VM migration plan to alleviate hot spots.

    Figure 10.    VM migration plan to alleviate hot spots – initial state

    Figure 11.    VM migration plan to alleviate hot spots – first step of remediation plan

    Figure 12.    VM migration plan to alleviate hot spots – remediation plan complete

    VM high availability

    AHV offers virtual machine high availability to ensure VM availability in a host outage. If a host fails, the VMs running on that host restart on healthy nodes throughout the cluster. Multiple high-availability configuration options are available to account for different cluster scenarios:

    By default, all AHV clusters provide best-effort high availability, even when you did not configure the cluster for high availability. Best-effort high availability works without reserving any resources and does not enforce admission control, so the capacity might not be sufficient to start all the VMs from the failed host.

    You can also configure an AHV cluster for high availability with resource reservation to guarantee that the resources required to restart VMs are always available. To enable guaranteed high-availability reservations, select the Enable HA Reservation checkbox.

    The Acropolis leader CVM restarts the VMs on the healthy hosts and tracks host health by monitoring connections to the libvirt on all cluster hosts. If the Acropolis leader becomes partitioned or isolated, or if it fails, the healthy portion of the cluster elects a new Acropolis leader from the Acropolis workers in the CVMs.

    The following diagram depicts three different high availability scenarios where VMs are restarted after a host failure.

     

    Figure 13.    AHV VM high availability preservation

    Advanced Processor Compatibility

    Advanced Processor Compatibility (APC) can streamline upgrades and transition clusters to the latest generation of CPUs. With APC, clusters are not limited by the slowest CPU. VMs can use APC to accurately identify and take advantage of the CPU features available to them, enabling improved migrations.

     

    Figure 14.    Advanced processor compatibility

    APC offers flexibility in multiple ways. Clusters can be leveled for consistent CPU presentation to guest VMs, which is the default behavior. You can also set a baseline CPU model on a per-VM basis for on-demand, cross-cluster live migrations to different hardware generations.

    Live migration

    Live migration allows the system to move VMs from one host to another while the VM is turned on without workload interruption, regardless of whether the administrator or an automatic process initiates the movement. Live migrations occur regularly in the cluster nodes, triggered by maintenance operations, ADS workload balancing, node expansion, or administrator-driven requests.

    You can also use live migration to migrate VMs to another physical cluster in the same location or in a different location to rebalance workloads, run maintenance operations, or avoid planned interruptions. For cross-cluster live migrations, we recommend a network with 5 ms of network latency, however it can support up to 40 ms of network latency.

    Start live migration with any of the following methods:

    • Put the AHV host in maintenance mode (VM evacuation)
    • Use the Prism UI
    • Use the aCLI (automatic, targeted, or maintenance mode)
    • Use the REST API (automatic, targeted, or maintenance mode)

    CPU types are abstracted from the VMs because AHV uses virtual CPUs (vCPUs) that are compatible between all nodes in the AHV cluster. If the destination AHV host has enough CPU cycles, you can migrate a VM.

    By default, live migration uses as much available bandwidth as required over the AHV host management interface, br0 and br0-up. To prevent resource contention, AHV limits the number of simultaneous automatic live-migration events to two. Additionally, you can restrict the bandwidth allocated for migration through the aCLI and the REST API using bandwidth_mbps=X during each migration. The following CVM aCLI example enforces a 100 Mbps limit when migrating a VM, slow-lane-VM1, to AHV host 10.10.10.11:

    acli vm.migrate slow-lane-VM1 bandwidth_mbps=100 host=10.10.10.11

    Note: A live migration between two Prism Central instances requires synchronous replication which is not yet available in Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform.

    Nutanix Guest Tools

    NGT is a set of software features installed in a VM and a Nutanix CVM. A Nutanix Guest Agent publishes information about the VM to the Nutanix cluster, such as guest operating system type, VM mobility status, and the Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS). The Nutanix Guest Agent is installed in both Windows and Linux guests.

     

    Figure 15.    NGT Communication Path

    Note: The guest VM ‘OS’ column in Prism Central requires Nutanix Guest Tools in the guest VM.

    Nutanix VSS hardware provider

    The Nutanix VSS hardware provider enables integration with native Nutanix data protection. The provider allows for application-consistent, VSS-based snapshots when using Nutanix protection domains and is supported with Windows guests.

    Self-Service Restore feature

    The Self-Service Restore feature enables Nutanix administrators or VM owners to mount snapshots directly to the VM they were taken from. This capability allows users to select specific files from a snapshot.

    The Self-Service Restore GUI and CLI are installed in Windows guests. The NGT CLI (ngtcli) runs the Self-Service Restore CLI. To access the Self-Service Restore GUI, open a browser, navigate to http://localhost:5000, and sign in with machine administrator credentials., and sign in with machine administrator credentials.

    Nutanix VirtIO drivers

    NGT installs Nutanix VirtIO drivers and provides the registry configuration necessary to support the migration or conversion of VMs bidirectionally between Nutanix AHV and VMware ESXi. AOS uses these drivers when performing Nutanix VM Mobility or Nutanix cluster conversion. The required drivers are installed in Windows guests.

    Windows guests require the installation of VirtIO drivers to run on Nutanix AHV and other KVM-based hypervisors.

Cluster Expansion

  • This section describes how to expand the NCI-C cluster with additional compute nodes and the external storage with additional Dell PowerFlex storage nodes.

    NCI-C cluster expansion

    Ensure that you adhere to the following guidelines when you expand the NCI-C cluster with additional compute nodes:

    • The AHV version of the new node is the same as that of the nodes in the NCI-C cluster.
    • The AOS version is lesser or equal to the AOS version of the nodes in the NCI-C cluster.

    Note: If the AHV version is different or the AOS version is higher than the AOS version of the existing nodes in the NCI-C cluster, the pre-checks fail. The system blocks the cluster expansion and instructs you to re-image the nodes with the appropriate AHV and AOS version using Foundation. After you re-image the node with the appropriate AHV and AOS version, use the expand cluster workflow to add the new Dell PowerFlex node to the NCI-C cluster.

    For information on how to expand the NCI-C cluster, see Expanding a Cluster in Prism Element Web Console Guide. Be sure to assign the correct uplinks for the Host/CVM network (typically vs0) as well as the PowerFlex data networking.

    External storage cluster expansion

    For information on how to expand the Dell PowerFlex external storage, see the Dell EMC PowerFlex Appliance Administration Guide.

    Snapshots

    Snapshots are performed in Prism Central, resulting in the creation of one additional volume per vDisk inside of PowerFlex external storage. These snapshots are a block image in the form of a storage volume or LUN used to instantaneously capture the state of a volume at a specific point in time. PowerFlex snapshots are thin-provisioned and are writable by default, although they can also be made immutable if required.

    All PowerFlex volumes that are created by Prism, including snapshots, are assigned to the Nutanix volume class. This ensures that any snapshots created by Prism cannot be removed or modified from within the PowerFlex Manager UI by a storage admin.

    Clones

    Clone operations are performed in Prism and result in the creation of two additional volumes per vDisk inside of PowerFlex external storage.

    Compression

    PowerFlex can provide inline data compression if needed. Compression is enabled by the use of Fine Granularity (FG) Storage Pools.

    The FG Storage Pool data layout allocates space at smaller units (4KB) than the default Medium Granularity (MG) Storage Pools, which allocates space in 1MB units. Use of Fine Granularity Storage Pools give better space efficiencies, especially when large numbers of snapshots are used. Compression is enabled on a per Storage Pool basis. If the benefits of storage compression are required, a Fine Granularity Storage Pool must be selected during the initial configuration of the External Storage from within Prism Element.

    PowerFlex does not provide data deduplication (dedupe) capabilities.

    VM configuration and application data performance and reliability

    Dell PowerFlex Distributed Mesh-Mirror architecture ensures there are always two copies of VM configuration and application data. This ensures availability in the event of unplanned hardware failure. VM configuration and application data is intelligently distributed across all the disk devices in each of the nodes within a storage pool. As more nodes are added, the overall performance increases linearly, without affecting application latencies. Adding more devices or nodes also decreases rebuild times during a failure situation – which means that PowerFlex heals itself more quickly as the system grows.

    PowerFlex automatically ensures that the two copies of each block of data that gets written to the Storage Pool reside on different SDS (storage) nodes, because Nutanix needs to be able to get a hold of the second copy of data if a device or a storage node that holds the first block fails at any time. Because the data is written across all the devices in all the nodes within a Storage Pool, this allows for fast IO response times, as all data is accessed in parallel.

    Figure 5.        Simplified view of a 4-Node PowerFlex system presenting 3 storage volumes

    Nutanix Disaster Recovery

    Performed in Prism Central, Nutanix Disaster Recovery offers an entity-centric automated approach to protect and recover applications using replication between both HCI and disaggregated architectures, or a blend of both. The following replication types are supported with external storage:

    • Asynchronous: One hour+ recovery point objective (RPO)
    • Synchronous: Zero recovery point objective (RPO)
    • Metro Availability:
    • Zero recovery point objective (RPO)
    • Near-zero recovery time objective (RTO)
    • Enables Cross-cluster Live Migration (CCLM) for zer-downtime live migration of entities across fault domains during planned failover events and workload balancing across clusters

    Nutanix Disaster Recovery works with sets of physically isolated locations called availability zones (AZs). An instance of Prism Central represents an AZ. One AZ is the primary AZ for an application, while one or more paired AZ is the recovery AZs. When paired, the primary AZ replicates the recovery points of the entities (guest VMs, volume groups, consistency groups) to the recovery AZs in the specified time intervals (RPO). This approach helps application recovery at any recovery AZs when a service disruption occurs at the primary AZ (for example, natural disasters or scheduled maintenance).

    Nutanix Disaster Recovery in Prism Central uses categories to group the guest VMs and automate the protection of the guest VMs as the application scales. Application recovery is more flexible with network mappings, an enforceable VM start sequence, and inter-stage delays. Application recovery can also be validated and tested without affecting your production workloads. Nearsync replication is not yet supported. Refer to this section in the Nutanix Bible to get more details about how protection policies and recovery plans work in Nutanix DR. Refer to the Nutanix Disaster Recovery Guide for more detailed information.

    VM Backup

    A variety of robust options exist to facilitate virtual machine backup and data protection. Dell PowerProtect Data Manager 19.22 or newer supports AHV workloads which can natively be backed up or restored from within Prism Central. For more information, see: PowerProtect Data Manager: Info Hub Product Documents and Information

    VM backup is also available via Nutanix integration with 3rd party backup applications, leveraging snapshots maintained on Dell PowerFlex external storage.

    Encryption

    Data Encryption at Rest (D@RE) is provided at the storage layer by PowerFlex Enterprise Encryption and KeyStore Services (PEEKS), which is a data encryption and key management solution previously known as Dell CloudLink. PowerFlex D@RE protects data from hacking, inside threats, and theft, ensuring that only those with authorized access are allowed to use the data. PowerFlex users can enable D@RE with the option to choose software encryption or key management for self-encrypting drives (SEDs). D@RE is configured when a Storage Pool is initially created by PowerFlex, therefore it is transparent to Prism.

    VM Migration

    Seamless VM migration across platforms is handled by Nutanix Move. Nutanix Move is a VM appliance that provides the ability to perform cross-hypervisor VM and files migration with minimal downtime. Nutanix Move can migrate VMs onto the Nutanix Cloud Platform from many hypervisors such as VMware ESXi and Microsoft Hyper-V, as well as AWS EC2, VMware Cloud (VMC) on AWS, and Microsoft Azure.

Dell PowerFlex and Nutanix Cloud Platform

  • This solution focuses on Nutanix Cloud Infrastructure Compute (NCI-C) comprising Compute, Networking, Disaster Recovery and Security. This is a new and specific license specifically tied to this architecture. NCI-C diverges from the hyperconverged consumption model that consolidates NCI-C components in addition to internal storage.

    Dell PowerFlex is a software-defined platform that integrates computing and storage with independent scaling capabilities. It supports multicloud environments and offers flexible management, which ensures performance, reliability, and scalability for diverse workloads.

    The integration of Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform (NCP) enables organizations to scale compute and storage resources independently. Nutanix AHV hypervisor and AOS operate on Dell PowerFlex compute servers, consuming storage from an external Dell PowerFlex Storage cluster. This setup leverages Dell’s software-defined PowerFlex storage alongside Nutanix AHV to optimize resource management. The architecture supports data protection, disaster recovery, and networking while facilitating hybrid cloud operations for scalable workloads. For more information on hardware and software specifications, see the Environment and System Requirements for NCI-C section.

Dell PowerFlex as external storage

  • The following section walks through adding Dell PowerFlex as external storage to the Nutanix instance, including all the prerequisites.

    Modify virtual switch

    During Foundation deployment, all active NIC ports will be bonded to the default virtual switch (vs0). In a typical NCI-C cluster configuration, two or more of the active NIC ports will be dedicated to storage. Therefore, after installation it will be necessary to modify the default virtual switch (vs0) to remove any active ports that will be dedicated to the Dell PowerFlex storage data networks. The instructions below guide the user through this process.

    Note: For this section, the following commands may be useful for identifying NIC ports:
    <SSH to host>lldpcli show neighbors
    <SSH to host>lldpctl
    <SSH to CVM>hostssh lldpctl
    <SSH to host>ovs-appctl bond/show | grep -v hash
    <SSH to CVM>hostssh ovs-appctl bond/show | grep -v hash
    <SSH to ToR switch>show lldp neighbors

    1. Navigate to the home screen and use the drop-down menu to select Settings. On the left-hand side, select Network Configuration from Network menu. Then click the Virtual Switch tab on the right-hand side. Next select the edit pencil which is boxed in green in the figure below.

    Figure 25.    Edit Virtual Switch

    1. In the Edit Virtual Switch screen, select the Quick configuration method and then Next. Scroll down to the hosts and use the arrow at the end of the host row which will expand all the NIC ports. Uncheck the ports you do not wish to be part of the management network. In the figure below and specific to this NCI-C cluster only, eth3 and eth4 are unchecked. Repeat this process for each host before clicking Save to finalize the modification.

    Figure 26.    Edit Virtual Switch Ethernet adapter deselection

    1. The operation will invoke a hypervisor rolling restart. The user can watch the progress by navigating to the Tasks menu in the drop-down menu at the top.
      Once complete, return to the virtual switch screen to create a new virtual switch using the available ports.

    Create a new virtual switch

    Follow these steps to create a new virtual switch. In this example the new virtual switch is specifically for SDC communication with the Dell PowerFlex storage.

    1. In the virtual switch screen select + Create VS.

    Figure 27.    Create Virtual Switch

    1. In the first screen add in a Virtual Switch Name, Description, and for this cluster we will change the MTU value to 9000 for jumbo frames support. Click Next.

    Figure 28.    Create Virtual Switch workflow

    1. Select the appropriate Bond Type based on the Ethernet fabric switch configuration and Nutanix networking best practices, Select Hosts (default All Hosts), and using the check boxes next to the host, select the NICs. Optionally use the Show, Uplink Port Speeds, and Select All toggles to speed up the selection process. In the example below, select eth3 and eth4 which are the NICs previously removed from the vs0 management switch. Click Create to complete the switch creation.

    Figure 29.    Selecting the bond type and NICs in the bond

    1. Use the newly created virtual switch to set up the external networks for the Dell PowerFlex SDC.

    External networks

    Before adding the Dell PowerFlex as external storage, create the Internal Interfaces necessary for communication with the SDC.

    1. Navigate to the home screen of Prism Element and use the drop-down menu to select Settings. On the left-hand side, select Network Configuration from Network menu. Then select the Internal Interfaces tab on the right-hand side. Click Create New Interface.

    Figure 30.    Create a new interface

    1. In the Interface Details tab enter a Descriptive Name and VLAN ID. Using the drop-down menu for the Virtual Switch, select the newly created virtual switch for SDC communication. Next click on + Create New IP Pool.
    2. Enter a Pool Name and Netmask and then click + Add an IP range. Enter a Start IP and End IP and click Save. This returns you to the IP Pool dialog and click Save again to return to the Create New Interface dialog.
    3. Click Next in step 4 which moves to the Feature Selection tab.
    4. Toggle the External Storage button, change the MTU value to 9000 for jumbo frames support, and click Save to complete the interface.

    Figure 31.    Create new interface workflow

    1. Repeat the process for additional VLANs. In this example, the SDC requires two VLANs.

    Figure 32.    Two internal interfaces have been created

    Add external storage

    Before adding Dell PowerFlex external storage, ensure the MDM Cluster is configured with Virtual IPs (VIPs). This can be verified in PowerFlex Manager by navigating to Resources | Highlight PowerFlex System row | View Details | MDM Cluster | Virtual IPs.

    Add Dell PowerFlex external storage by following the steps below.

    1. Navigate to the home screen of Prism Element and under Storage Summary on the left-hand side, select + Set up External Storage followed by + Attach External Storage.

    Figure 33.    Set up External Storage in Prism Element

    1. When entering the wizard, the External Storage Vendor will default to Dell PowerFlex as the only fully integrated external storage, as of this writing. First, be sure that network segmentation is set up specifically for external storage. This should have been completed prior to adding external storage. See section External Networks for more detail. The networks will be displayed in the Network Setup (Optional) section at the bottom, though it will not be optional in a properly configured Dell PowerFlex since the SDC should be on a separate network/VLAN. This network(s) is specifically for SDC communication back to the Dell PowerFlex cluster. In the example below, there are two data networks, vlan151 and vlan152.
    2. In the SDC Installation section, add the .json and .zip files and click Install.

    Figure 34.    Initial setup page for adding external storage

    1. Once installation of the SDC is complete, there will be a green checkmark next to each field. Click Next.

    Figure 35.    SDC files have been uploaded

    1. In Connection Details, enter a Name for the Dell PowerFlex, the IP address of the PowerFlex Manager (API Endpoint) and a PowerFlex Manager Username and Password having the StorageAdmin or higher role. Click Next. Nutanix will attempt to connect to the PowerFlex Manager. If it fails an error message will appear. Resolve before proceeding.

    Figure 36.    Connection details for PowerFlex Manager are provided

    Note: A service account is recommended for the external storage connection. The service account must have the PowerFlex Manager StorageAdmin role or above. If the service account password is changed or rotated on a recurring basis, it must be updated in both PowerFlex Manager and Prism.

    1. In the Storage Details screen, use the drop-down menus to select the PowerFlex Protection Domain and the Storage Pool Name. Only one of each may be selected. Click Attach to complete.

    Figure 37.    Attach External Storage workflow Protection Domain and Storage Pool selection

    Note: Only one Dell PowerFlex external storage, Protection Domain, and Storage Pool may be attached to an NCI-C cluster. However, a single PowerFlex storage cluster will support multiple NCI-C clusters, as well as all other host types traditionally supported by PowerFlex.

    After external storage has been added, a Storage Container will be created automatically and can be immediately used. This Storage Container will be tied to the Protection Domain and Storage Pool specified above and can be used going forward to store all VMs, templates, images, OVAs. Although it is not necessary, additional Storage Containers may be created with different Advertised Capacity characteristics. However, they will be tied to the same Protection Domain and Storage Pool specified above.

    Figure 38.    The PowerFlex Storage Container is automatically created, and available Storage Containers are shown in Prism Element

    The NCI-C cluster will immediately begin consuming the external storage after it has been added. This is accomplished with the dynamic provisioning of per-node volumes. These will be covered in more detail in a later section.

    The CVM, which had previously been provisioned on the BOSS card, will now use external PowerFlex storage for the bulk of its operations going forward. However, the CVM will continue to use BOSS card storage for logs and binary uploads.

    After adding the external storage to the system, the Health and Cluster Resiliency/ Fault Tolerance Status applets exist in a Critical state for about 2 hours, and post this timeline, the system turns to Healthy (Green) status.

    Figure 39.    External storage health

Dell PowerFlex deployment architectures

  • Dell PowerFlex software-defined storage offers flexibility of deployment architecture to help best meet the specific deployment and architectural requirements. Dell PowerFlex can natively be deployed in a disaggregated (Independent) architectures. Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform uses a disaggregated (independent) architecture.

    Figure 3.        Dell PowerFlex deployment architectures

    Note: Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform uses a two-layer (independent) architecture.

    Independent architecture

    In an independent architecture, or two-layer architecture, some nodes provide storage capacity and host datasets while other, separate, and independent nodes, host applications and workloads. Compute and storage resources can be scaled independently by adding nodes to the cluster. This separation of compute and storage resources can also help minimize software licensing costs in certain situations. And this architecture can be ideal for hosting high-performance high-value databases and application workloads.

Dell PowerFlex family

  • Dell PowerFlex software-defined infrastructure enables broad consolidation across the data center, encompassing almost any type of workload and architecture. The software- defined architecture offers automation and programmability of the complete infrastructure and provides scalability, performance, and resiliency to enable effortless adherence to stringent workload SLAs.

    The Dell PowerFlex family provides a foundation that combines compute and high- performance storage resources in a managed unified fabric. Dell PowerFlex comes in flexible deployment options (rack, appliance, or custom nodes and in the public cloud) that enable independent (disaggregated) architectures. Dell PowerFlex is ideal for high-performance applications and databases, building an agile private/hybrid cloud, or consolidating resources in heterogeneous environments.

    Figure 1.        The PowerFlex family

    The platform supports a broad range of operating environments – bare metal operating systems, hypervisors, and container platforms – simultaneously with a unified infrastructure platform and management. By allowing users to flexibly mix these architectures in a single deployment, PowerFlex enables you to deploy, scale, and evolve all your applications to meet your business objectives.

    Figure 2.        Consolidation: OS, Hypervisor, Platform Support

    Dell PowerFlex software components

    Software is the key differentiation in the Dell PowerFlex offering. Dell PowerFlex software components not only provide software-defined storage services but also help simplify infrastructure management and orchestration. This software enables comprehensive IT Operational Management (ITOM) and Life Cycle Management (LCM) capabilities that span compute as well as storage infrastructure, from BIOS and Firmware to nodes, software, and networking.

    Dell PowerFlex

    Dell PowerFlex is the software foundation of Dell PowerFlex software-defined infrastructure. It is a scale-out block storage service that is designed to deliver flexibility, elasticity, and simplicity with predictable high performance and resiliency at scale. For more details, see Dell PowerFlex specifications.

    Dell PowerFlex Manager

    Dell PowerFlex Manager is the software component in the Dell PowerFlex family that enables ITOM automation and LCM capabilities for Dell PowerFlex systems. Starting with Dell PowerFlex 4.0, the unified Dell PowerFlex Manager brings together three separate components used in previous releases – Dell PowerFlex Manager, the core Dell PowerFlex UI, and the Dell PowerFlex gateway. The new Dell PowerFlex UI runs in Kubernetes and embraces a modern development framework.

Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform architecture

  • Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform (NCP) is deployed using a disaggregated architecture, as shown in the following illustration.

    • Compute Layer: A Nutanix Cloud Infrastructure Compute (NCI-C) cluster with AOS and AHV running on Dell PowerFlex compute-only nodes.
    • Storage Layer: A Dell PowerFlex cluster operating in a storage-only model, compatible with PowerFlex configurations. This cluster provides block storage and related services as shown in the dashed blue box in Figure 4.

    Figure 4.        Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform architecture

    The Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform architecture contains no internal storage within the Nutanix compute only nodes. In this disaggregated architecture, the compute cluster accesses storage over the Ethernet fabric from the external PowerFlex storage cluster via the SDC that is installed on every node of the NCI-C cluster.

    When Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform is deployed, the Nutanix software stack is hosted on the PowerFlex compute only nodes. The NCI-C cluster nodes consume storage from the PowerFlex storage cluster.

Deploying VMs

  • There are a variety of methods available to deploy virtual machines on the NCI-C cluster. Most methods involve using Prism Central workflows. However, command line and API can also be used, as well as VM migration from private, hybrid, and public clouds using Nutanix Move.

    Choose from the following options to create VMs in AHV:

    • Create an empty VM and install the operating system and needed applications.
    • Create a VM from an existing VM using the clone feature.
    • Create a VM from an existing VM snapshot using the clone feature.
    • Import a VM from a VM disk image using the image service or network share.
    • Import a VM using cross-hypervisor disaster recovery or hypervisor conversion.

    The following table outlines virtual machine driver requirements with respect to VirtIO and Nutanix Guest Tools. For more information and best practices, refer to the Nutanix AHV Best Practices documentation.

    Table 9.      Virtual Machine Driver requirements

    AHV VM Operation

    VirtIO Required

    NGT Required

    Additional Information

    Create New VM: Windows

    Yes

    No

    VirtIO driver installation is required. The Nutanix Guest Tools (NGT) software is optional.

    Create New VM: Linux

    Yes

    No

    VirtIO support in the Linux kernel is required and enabled for all AHV-supported Linux distributions by default. The NGT software is optional.

    External Import via

    Image Service or

    Copied to Active

    Directory Federation

    Service (ADFS):

    Windows

    Yes

    No

    VirtIO is required in the image (for example, VMDK, qcow) uploaded to the image service or copied to ADFS.

    The NGT software is optional.

    External Import via

    Image Service or

    Copied to ADFS: Linux

    Yes

    No

    VirtIO support in the Linux kernel is

    required for the image uploaded to image

    service or copied to ADFS. All AHV supported Linux distributions have

    VirtIO enabled by default. The NGT

    software is optional.

    Cross-Hypervisor

    DR or Conversion:

    Windows

    Yes

    Yes

    VirtIO and NGT are required.

    Cross-Hypervisor DR

    or Conversion: Linux

    Yes

    Yes

    VirtIO support in the VM Linux kernel and

    NGT are required.

    PowerFlex supports up to 126 snapshots per volume, which limits the number of times you can clone/snapshot any virtual disks. As a best practice, it is recommended you limit the number of clones per image uploaded in Prism Central. For example, if you want to deploy 100 VM’s from the same image, the recommendation would be to only clone that image up to 50 times so that you have enough capacity for snapshots. Once you’ve reached 50 VMs, you can upload the image again with a different name, which results in a new volume being created on PowerFlex. You can resume creating VMs by cloning the new image to avoid reaching the snapshot limit. Once you reach the 126 snapshot limit, snapshots and clone operations will fail with error indicating you have reached the PowerFlex snapshot limit. Certain applications, such as VDI, will need to be sized appropriately based on these defined limits. See Nutanix KB-17640 for more information.

Deployment

  • Nutanix Kubernetes Platform support for external storage architecture was added with the AOS 7.5 release. NKP is deployed on an existing Nutanix compute cluster managed by Prism Central. For a greenfield environment, the prerequisites and high level order of installation would look like the following:

    1. Deploy PowerFlex storage infrastructure
    2. Deploy Nutanix compute nodes with AOS 7.5 or newer and AHV 11 or newer
      1. When sized properly, Nutanix compute nodes can run mixed workloads of VMs and NKP or be dedicated to NKP
    3. Attach external PowerFlex storage to compute nodes
    4. Deploy Prism Central 7.5 or newer
    5. Deploy NKP management and managed cluster(s)

    The purpose of this section is to assume steps one through four above are completed. Focus from this point forward will be on cluster types and the deployment of the management and managed (workload) clusters.

    In a single-cluster environment, the initial NKP cluster is a stand-alone cluster. It is self-managed and capable of handling its own scaling, upgrades, and life-cycle. In this single-cluster environment, all workloads are run on the single NKP cluster. If more than one NKP cluster is needed, Nutanix recommends using a multi-cluster environment.

    Figure 53.    Single-Cluster Environment

    In a multi-cluster environment, three cluster types are supported:

    • Management Cluster (All NKP editions): Is the cluster where you install NKP, and it is self-managed. In a multi-cluster environment, the Management cluster also manages other clusters. Customers are encouraged to run workloads on Managed and Attached clusters, not on the Management cluster except in single-cluster environments.
    • Managed Cluster (All NKP editions): Also called an “NKP cluster,” this is a type of workload cluster that you can create with NKP. Examples include Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP), Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS), and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS). The NKP Management cluster manages its infrastructure, its life cycle, and its applications.
    • Attached Cluster (NKP Ultimate only): This is a type of managed cluster that is created outside of NKP but is then connected to the NKP Management Cluster so that NKP can manage its applications. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) is one example The lifecycle will not be managed by NKP.

    Figure 54.    Multi-Cluster Environment

    The NKP management cluster deployment is flexible in that it can be deployed in a few different ways, including:

    1. Deploy using Prism Central Marketplace. This is a graphical user interface driven deployment introduced in Prism Central 7.5 which avoids the need for command line knowledge and related tools, as well as a Linux jump host (a bastion host is automatically created and decommissioned using this method). This deployment method gets NKP up and running quickly. Prism Central access to the internet is required otherwise a local registry is needed.
    2. Deploy using the Nutanix Kubernetes Platform Guide. This is a comprehensive deployment method with flexibility for any and all supported installation types. Requires Linux command line and related tooling knowledge. Access to the internet is required otherwise a local registry is needed.
    3. Deploy using nkp-quickstart at GitHub. This is an immensely streamlined variation of the Nutanix Kubernetes Platform Guide method above. It takes a 1,356 page manual and boils the deployment down to a few easy steps for a basic installation. This deployment method gets NKP up and running quickly. A jump host is created, NKP tools are downloaded and installed, and the NKP cluster is deployed. Access to the internet is required otherwise a local registry is needed.

    Note: NKP can be deployed in air-gapped or non-air-gapped environments. For more information, refer to the Nutanix Kubernetes Platform Guide.

    Management cluster deployment

    In the next series of steps, the management cluster will be deployed using Prism Central Marketplace.

    In Prism Central, navigate to the Admin Center and then Marketplace. Find Nutanix Kubernetes Platform and choose Get.

    Figure 55.    Nutanix Kubernetes Platform in Prism Central Marketplace

    Provide a valid NKP Cluster Name avoiding illegal characters. The SSH Public Key would come from the output of ssh-keygen on a Linux host or similar tool. Tick the box to apply the same SSH config to cluster nodes.

    Figure 56.    Name and Access

    Provide appropriate Prism Central credentials and Prism Element cluster.

    Figure 57.    Provider

    Choose a compatible nkp-rocky release from the OS image pulldown menu. This image would have been downloaded from Nutanix and uploaded into Prism in order to be available for selection here. Only images compatible with a Prism Marketplace deployment will be shown in the pulldown menu.

    Figure 58.    Resources

    Choose the PowerFlex Storage Container. This Storage Container will be associated with the storage class used to deploy containerized applications on the management cluster.

    Figure 59.    Storage

    Provide the subnet, control plane endpoint, and load balancer range.

    Figure 60.    Network & Proxy

    Provide an appropriate registry mirror and credentials necessary to authenticate and avoid rate limiting restrictions on image pulls.

    Figure 61.    Registry

    The deployment will create a temporary bastion host as well as the control plane and worker nodes. After several minutes, the bastion host will be removed and the management cluster deployment will complete.

    Workload cluster deployment

    In the next series of steps, the managed (workload) cluster will be deployed using Kommander. Kommander is deployed automatically with the management cluster and typically consumes the first available IP address in the load balancer range provided. The Kommander dashboard URL and credentials (as well as the KubeConfig for the management cluster) can be found in Prism Central. Navigate to the Admin Center | My Apps, then click on the Manage link under the NKP deployment.

    Figure 62.    Kommander dashboard URL, credentials, and KubeConfig

    In Kommander, choose Create Cluster.

    Figure 63.    Create Cluster

    Provide a valid workload cluster name. Avoid using illegal characters.

    Figure 64.    Cluster Name

    Provide the same SSH Public Key used in a previous step when creating the management cluster. The AOS cluster, subnet, and OS image for the control plane nodes must also be provided.

    Figure 65.    SSH Public Key and control plane details

    Specify the control plane endpoint IP for the workload cluster as well as the AOS cluster and subnet for the worker nodes.

    Figure 66.    Control plane and worker node details

    Choose the OS image for the worker nodes.

    Figure 67.    Worker node details

    Choose the PowerFlex Storage Container. This Storage Container will be associated with the storage class used to deploy containerized applications on the workload cluster.

    Figure 68.    Storage container selection

    A range of available IP addresses must be provided for the workload cluster load balancer. Provide an appropriate registry mirror and credentials necessary to authenticate and avoid rate limiting restrictions on image pulls.

    Figure 69.    Workload cluster networking and image registry mirror details

    After several minutes, the managed (workload) cluster deployment will complete. To manage the workload cluster and deploy containerized applications using kubectl, the kubeconfig for the workload cluster can be downloaded from Kommander.

    Figure 70.    Download the kubeconfig for the workload cluster in Kommander

Flow Network Security

  • Flow Network Security (FNS) is the next-generation Nutanix micro segmentation solution that has an enhanced policy model, advanced policy operation, enterprise readiness. It features (v4 APIs, RBAC and improved scale performance and resiliency) with Network Controller, and Network Controller-enabled subnet VLANs and VPC as pre-requisites. Refer to this section to see how it works and how to implement it.

    Flow Network Security policies protect VMs on AHV using simple text-based categories that apply to the VM. Categories and policies are centrally managed from Prism, but the firewall enforcement is distributed to the AHV nodes in the cluster closest to the VMs.

    FNS policies provide east-west protection for VMs inside VLANs or even to VMs inside a VPC network.

Flow Virtual Networking

  • Flow Virtual Networking, powered by Network Controller, drives network virtualization to offer a seamless network experience with enhanced security. Flow Virtual Networking VPCs (Virtual Private Clouds) deliver software-defined overlay networks with multi-tiered virtualization-based routing.

    Flow Virtual Networking is a software-defined networking solution that provides multi-tenant isolation, self-service provisioning, and IP address preservation using VPCs, subnets, and other virtual components that are separate from the physical network, for the AHV clusters. It integrates tools to deploy networking features like Virtual LANs, Virtual Private Cloud (VPC), Virtual Private Network (VPN), Layer 2 Virtual Network Extension using VPN or Virtual Tunnel End Point (VTEP), Border Gateway Protocol sessions to support flexible app-driven networking that focuses on VMs and applications.

    Flow Virtual Networking deploys the following components to manage software-defined network virtualization:

    Network Controller

    The Network Controller is the networking component of Prism Central that manages and controls configuration, monitoring, and optimization of network resources for Flow Virtual Networking VPCs and VLAN subnets. It provides programmability, automation, and centralized control for configuring and managing network flows.

    Network Controller is necessary to use centralized VLAN management, Flow Virtual Networking, and Flow Network Security Next Generation.

    Network Gateway

    The Network Gateway appliance is available along with the Network Controller when you install Prism Central. Network Gateway VMs are used to create VPN, VTEP, or BGP gateways to connect subnets using VPN connections, Layer 2 subnet extensions over VPN or VTEP, or BGP sessions. To learn more about its functionality refer to this section in the Nutanix Bible.

    Subnet Extension is a valuable tool to perform layer 2 extension between different types of virtual networks to facilitate VM migration. Subnet Extension between on-prem sites or even the cloud can be an important part of any migration strategy.

Hardware/ Software

  • The following prerequisites must be met before implementing Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform.

    Storage node

    Dell PowerFlex rack or appliance nodes are supported for the storage layer. Dell PowerFlex custom nodes and software-only deployments are not supported. Dell requires a minimum of three storage nodes for the implementation.

    The following Dell PowerFlex storage node models are supported:

    • Dell PowerFlex R650
    • Dell PowerFlex R750
    • Dell PowerFlex R660
    • Dell PowerFlex R760
    • Dell PowerFlex R670
    • Dell PowerFlex R770

    Note: PowerFlex supports providing external storage to more than one NCI-C cluster. However, an NCI-C cluster may be attached to only one PowerFlex Protection Domain and Storage Pool.

    Compute node

    For production and non-production environments, a minimum of three identical compute nodes are required in the Nutanix cluster. Five compute nodes are required to support Cluster Redundancy Factor RF3 and Cluster Fault Tolerance 2N/2D.

    Note: In a three or four compute node configuration, more than one simultaneous node outage will affect cluster availability. One or two node compute configurations are not supported.

    The following Dell PowerFlex compute node models are supported for NCI-C deployments:

    • Dell PowerFlex R640
    • Dell PowerFlex R740
    • Dell PowerFlex R650
    • Dell PowerFlex R750
    • Dell PowerFlex R660
    • Dell PowerFlex R760
    • Dell PowerFlex R670
    • Dell PowerFlex R770
    • Dell PowerFlex R6525
    • Dell PowerFlex R7525
    • Dell PowerFlex R6625
    • Dell PowerFlex R7625
    • Dell PowerFlex R6725
    • Dell PowerFlex R7725

    Note: AMD based nodes are only available as compute only (CO) nodes. They are not available for storage only (SO) nodes.

    CPU

    NCI-C nodes require a minimum of 16 physical CPU cores per socket.

    Memory

    The minimum memory per NCI-C node is 256GB.

    Network

    Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform requires minimum 25GbE networking, 100GbE and Jumbo Frames are preferred. NIC type must be NVIDIA/Mellanox CX5/CX6 and/or Broadcom. NIC types cannot be mixed per node, nor per NCI-C cluster.

    Trunk ports or Link Aggregation Group (LAG) configurations are supported. In the case of a LAG, Dynamic Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) is required. Static LACP is not supported.

    CVM

    The standard CVM configuration is 16 vCPUs and 32GB RAM. In some configurations, Foundation may allocate 12 vCPUs and that is supported. It is impossible to power on a CVM if threads have to cross a socket.

    Software

    Listed here are the software requirements for both Dell PowerFlex and Nutanix Cloud Platform.

    Dell PowerFlex

    • Dell PowerFlex 4.5.4 or higher
    • Dell PowerFlex Manager 4.6.2 or higher
    • Dell PowerFlex SDC for Nutanix
    • From a device that has public internet access, go to the Downloads page of the Nutanix support portal.
    • Choose PowerFlex SDC from the pulldown menu.
    • Download the latest Dell PowerFlex SDC zip file and metadata.json file.

    Nutanix

    • Foundation 5.8.1 or higher
    • AOS version 7.1 or higher
    • AHV version 10.1 or higher
    • PC 2024.3.1 or higher

Installation

  • The deployment of Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform consists of a few steps performed in order. Nutanix Foundation is used to deploy the Nutanix Cloud Infrastructure Compute cluster nodes.

    Nutanix Foundation

    Foundation is a Nutanix provided tool leveraged for bootstrapping, imaging, and deployment of Nutanix clusters. The imaging process will install the AOS and AHV components.

    Foundation can be installed on an OS or deployed as a VM appliance. In this example, Foundation is deployed as a VM appliance on an existing VMware ESXi host. Foundation requires layer 2 or layer 3 network connectivity to both the iDRAC network and the host/CVM network of the NCI-C nodes. Additional vNICs and IP addresses can be assigned to the Foundation VM to meet networking requirements.

    Once the VM is deployed, it will attempt to discover a DHCP server for each of its vNICs. If a DHCP server is not available, assign a static TCP/IP configuration to the vNIC(s). Access the Foundation interface remotely via a web browser. Alternatively, launch the Foundation interface locally using the Nutanix Foundation icon on the desktop. This will start Mozilla Firefox and open the default web page http://localhost:8000/gui/index.html.

    The Create Deployment workflow will guide you through a typical installation.

    The following figure shows the first page of the wizard. Here you will enter the subnets for the nodes as well as the iDRACs. Click Next to move to step 2.

    Figure 16.    Nutanix Foundation start page

    1. The column headings for compute nodes are defined as follows:
    • NODE – the physical location of the node in the block/chassis
    • IPMI IP – the IP address for the iDRAC
    • HOST IP – the IP address assigned to the AHV host
    • CVM IP – the IP address assigned to the CVM running on the host
    • HOSTNAME OF HOST – Arbitrary name of the AHV host

    Tick the box indicating external storage. A NODE ROLE of “Compute” will automatically be provided. Use NODE A for a single node block/chassis. In the right-hand corner of the image note that, under the Tools drop-down, there are several options available. One of these is Range Autofill which will sequence the IPs starting from the top.

    This provides an efficient way to complete the table cells when there are more nodes in the NCI-C cluster. Provide three IP addresses and the HOSTNAME for each node. Click Next.

    Figure 17.    Nutanix Foundation nodes page

    Note: Do not use Foundation to image PowerFlex storage nodes. Data loss will occur.

    1. In the AOS/Hypervisor step you must provide the software to install. At the top select Upload New AOS Binary and provide the .tar file. Next, select the Hypervisor Type, in this example AHV is used. Finally click  Upload New AHV Binary and provide the .iso file. Click Next to proceed.

    Figure 18.    Nutanix Foundation AOS/Hypervisor page

    Note: Foundation will configure the CVM vCPUs. The preferred vCPU count for the CVM is 16 but a minimum of 12 vCPUs is supported.

    1. Provide a Cluster Name, Cluster Fault Tolerance (available RF depends on number of nodes deployed), Cluster Virtual IP, NTP Servers, and finally DNS Servers. Click Next.

    Figure 19.    Nutanix Foundation cluster page

    1. Choose a Cluster Lockdown preference. In this example, SSH Using Password is chosen. Click Next.

    Figure 20.    Nutanix Foundation security page

    1. In the final step of the wizard, provide iDRAC credentials for each NCI-C node. The iDRAC is used to deploy AOS and AHV on each NCI-C node. Click Start to begin the installation.

    Figure 21.    Nutanix Foundation IPMI page

    1. A warning requires acknowledgement that the browser machine will not sleep during the installation (not shown). The deployment process takes about 45 minutes to an hour depending on the hardware configuration. The Deployment History page provides both summary and detailed status during and post deployment. Ensure all operations are completed successfully before proceeding.

    Figure 22.    Nutanix Foundation Deployment History page with successful completed deployment

    Initial Login

    An Open Prism link is provided on the Deployment History page to access Prism Element. Prism Element may also be opened by navigating to the following URL: https://<ANY_CVM_IP>:9440. Prism Element prompts for an admin password change at first login. Accept the EULA and enable Pulse (if possible).

    Figure 23.    Prism Element UI with Pulse enable or disable feature

    Note: The maximum age of the admin account password before a rotation is forced (default 60 days) can be configured via SSH into Prism Central with the following command:
    allssh sudo chage -M <MAX_DAYS> admin

    Previously used passwords are “remembered” in:
    /etc/security/opasswd

    A locked admin account can be unlocked with the following command:
    sudo faillock --user admin --reset

    After navigating through these screens, the dashboard appears with another pop-up dialog to set up external storage. Because of the additional network steps needed, click I’ll do this later.

    Figure 24.    Prompt to set up external storage in Prism Element

Lifecycle Management

  • Both Dell PowerFlex and Nutanix Cloud Platform offer fully integrated and comprehensive Lifecycle Management (LCM) of qualified components for their respective architectures. These powerful features combine to provide end to end Lifecycle Management of both software and hardware across storage and compute nodes.

    PowerFlex storage only nodes

    In the PowerFlex Manager UI, storage only nodes have a managed state of Managed. This indicates that PowerFlex Manager controls PowerFlex software and firmware in a turnkey fashion with no interruption to workloads. The state of the nodes can be seen in Figure 6.

    Nutanix compute only nodes

    In PowerFlex Manager, PowerFlex NCI-C nodes have a managed state of Reserved. This indicates that PowerFlex Manager can upgrade the firmware on a compute node after it has been placed in maintenance mode, bringing it into compliance with a Release Certification Matrix/Intelligent Catalog (RCM/IC). Maintenance mode evacuates the workloads, so they are not impacted by the LCM process. Prism Central LCM manages Nutanix software on NCI-C nodes including AOS and AHV. At the time of this writing, the PowerFlex SDC is signed by Nutanix, downloaded from portal.nutanix.com, and deployed to the NCI-C cluster using Prism Element. The Nutanix software and the PowerFlex SDC are qualified and upgraded together in lock step with each other.

    Figure 6.        PowerFlex compliant storage only and non-compliant compute only nodes needing LCM as seen in PowerFlex Manager

    Note: Compute only nodes should be placed in maintenance mode before software or firmware updates are applied.

Management

  • NKP clusters are upstream and CNCF compatible meaning they can be managed traditionally using kubectl on any network host with the kubectl tool and the kubeconfig for the Kubernetes cluster to be managed.

    Kubectl commands can be performed against a given cluster by providing the
    --kubeconfig flag for each command:

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart ~]$ kubectl cluster-info --kubeconfig=/home/nutanix/nkp-quickstart/nkp-workload-kubeconfig.conf

    Kubernetes control plane is running at https://172.105.16.55:6443

    CoreDNS is running at https://172.105.16.55:6443/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/services/kube-dns:dns/proxy

    Alternatively, KUBECONFIG can be exported and used for the duration of the kubectl session without having to repeatedly specify it for each kubectl command:

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart ~]$ export KUBECONFIG=/home/nutanix/nkp-quickstart/nkp-workload-kubeconfig.conf

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart ~]$ kubectl get nodes

    NAME                                  STATUS   ROLES           AGE    VERSION

    nkp-workload-kvw82-6pd7b              Ready    control-plane   171m   v1.34.1

    nkp-workload-kvw82-d8tnx              Ready    control-plane   173m   v1.34.1

    nkp-workload-kvw82-fbf7l              Ready    control-plane   169m   v1.34.1

    nkp-workload-md-0-g9m45-nw8nm-8mndb   Ready    <none>          172m   v1.34.1

    nkp-workload-md-0-g9m45-nw8nm-gc9dn   Ready    <none>          172m   v1.34.1

    nkp-workload-md-0-g9m45-nw8nm-mgr5k   Ready    <none>          172m   v1.34.1

    nkp-workload-md-0-g9m45-nw8nm-vvsrb   Ready    <none>          172m   v1.34.1

    Kubectl will be used throughout the lifecycle of an NKP workload cluster to perform all of the common tasks a delegated administrator or devops engineer would use it for in their role. Examples include deploying and decommissioning cloud native and load balanced applications, scaling replica sets, provisioning and decommissioning persistent volumes, and so on.

Migration with Nutanix Move

  • Nutanix Move is a VM appliance that can perform cross-hypervisor VM and files migration with minimal downtime during final cutover. Nutanix Move can migrate VMs onto the Nutanix Cloud Platform from many hypervisors such as ESXi and Hyper-V as well as from AWS EC2, VMware Cloud (VMC) on AWS and Microsoft Azure. The Move architecture consists of software components that together provide the functionality of VM migration. They consist of:

    The management server

    The management server maintains source and target cluster information, migration plan details, and status. It also allows APIs and the UI to create and manage migration plans.

    Agents for source and target

    The source agent is a platform-specific (ESXi, Hyper-V, AHV, or cloud) software component that schedules migration copy requests through disk readers. It collects source cluster and VM details and helps you select the VMs to migrate using the management server UI.

    Disk readers and writers

    Disk reader processes use source-specific APIs to read data and coordinate with disk writer processes to complete outstanding copy operations. The disk reader checkpoints copy operations to handle failures and resume operations as needed.

    Figure 51.    Distributed architecture of Nutanix Move

    Nutanix Move for VMware ESXi architecture is detailed in the Nutanix Bible here.

    Nutanix Move can also be used to migrate VMware ESXi VMs currently running on Dell PowerFlex storage to Nutanix NCI-C cluster attached to the same Dell PowerFlex storage cluster. This involves VM and data copy where the VMs are moved from an ESXi cluster to a Nutanix NCI-C cluster. Although the source and destination PowerFlex storage can be the same, it still involves copying data from its source storage constructs to the NCI-C cluster volumes on the destination storage pool. Details about how to perform ESXi to AHV migrations using Nutanix Move including adding source and destination clusters, creating a migration plan, and then performing data migration and cutover are detailed here.

    Move supports VM migration from the following sources to targets, where the first platform is the source, and the second platform is the target:

    • VMware ESXi (legacy infrastructure or Nutanix) to AHV
    • VMware ESXi (legacy infrastructure or Nutanix) to VMware ESXi on Nutanix
    • VMware ESXi to Nutanix Cloud Clusters (NC2) on AWS
    • VMware ESXi to NC2 on Microsoft Azure
    • VMware Cloud (VMC) on AWS to AHV
    • VMC on AWS to NC2 on AWS
    • VMC to ESXi on Nutanix
    • Microsoft Hyper-V to AHV
    • Microsoft Hyper-V to VMware ESXi on Nutanix
    • Microsoft Hyper-V to NC2 on AWS
    • Microsoft Hyper-V to NC2 on Azure
    • AWS EC2 to AHV
    • AWS EC2 to VMware ESXi on Nutanix
    • AWS EC2 to NC2 on AWS
    • Microsoft Azure Cloud to AHV
    • Microsoft Azure Cloud to VMware ESXi on Nutanix
    • Microsoft Azure Cloud to NC2 on Azure
    • Nutanix AHV to Nutanix AHV
    • Nutanix AHV to AWS EC2
    • Nutanix AHV to Microsoft Azure Cloud
    • Nutanix AHV to NC2 on AWS/Azure
    • NC2 on AWS to Nutanix AHV

    Migration from VMware vSphere to Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform

    For existing disaggregated deployments Dell PowerFlex storage with the ESXi hypervisor, you can migrate to Dell PowerFlex storage with the AHV hypervisor. Prepare and migrate VMs running on the ESXi hypervisor to the AHV hypervisor by using Nutanix Move. Nutanix does not support the online migration of ESXi VMs. Nutanix only supports offline migration of ESXi VMs. For more information on offline migration from the ESXi hypervisor to the AHV hypervisor, see Nutanix Move User Guide.

Nutanix AHV

  • The native Nutanix hypervisor, AHV represents a unique approach to virtualization that offers powerful virtualization capabilities needed to deploy and manage enterprise applications. AHV provides value by integrating native virtualization along with networking, infrastructure, and operations management with a single intuitive interface - Nutanix Prism.

    Virtualization teams find AHV easy to learn and transition to from legacy virtualization solutions with familiar workflows for VM operations, live migration, VM high availability, and virtual network management. AHV includes resiliency features, including high availability and dynamic scheduling without the need for additional licensing

    Security is integral to every aspect of the system from the ground up. AHV incorporates the optional Flow Network Security and Flow Virtual Networking, allowing easy access to hypervisor-based network micro-segmentation and advanced software-defined networking.

    To get more details around AHV and its various components refer to this tech note and to learn about AHV architecture, you can refer to this section in the Nutanix Bible.

Nutanix Disaster Recovery

  • Nutanix Disaster Recovery offers an entity-centric automated approach to protect and recover applications. It uses categories to group the guest VMs and automate the protection of the guest VMs as the application scales. Application recovery is more flexible with network mappings, an enforceable VM start sequence, and inter-stage delays. Application recovery can also be validated and tested without affecting production workloads. 

    This solution provides an asynchronous (RPO 1 hour) or synchronous (RPO 0) replication schedule. Nearsync replication is not yet supported. Refer to this section in Nutanix Bible for more details about how protection policies and recovery plans work in Nutanix DR. Refer here for a complete guide to set up Nutanix DR.

    Note: Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform supports Prism Central based Asynchronous or Synchronous Disaster Recovery between both HCI and disaggregated architectures, or a blend of both.

Overview

  • Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform is a modern enterprise virtualization platform that provides a two-tier, or disaggregated, architecture. It brings together Dell PowerFlex storage and the Nutanix Acropolis Hypervisor (AHV) to deliver a best-of-breed virtualization environment that is designed to keep pace with modern IT operations.

    This paper provides a technical overview of the solution as well as the individual components and how they are integrated to create a powerful virtualization platform for PowerFlex customers.

Overview

  • Containers and container management are changing the way applications and services are developed and delivered to businesses globally. In most instances, automated deployment, scaling, management, and orchestration of containerized applications becomes a necessity. Kubernetes is an open-source orchestrator for deploying containerized applications. Originally developed by Google, Kubernetes was inspired by a decade of experience deploying scalable, reliable systems in containers by using application-oriented APIs.

    Nutanix Kubernetes Platform (NKP) transforms a Nutanix compute cluster into developer-ready infrastructure with the ability to run both management and managed Kubernetes clusters. In the Dell PowerFlex with Nutanix Cloud Platform disaggregated architecture, PowerFlex provides the high performing and highly scalable block storage used by NKP clusters. Combining NKP and Dell PowerFlex is a good fit for modernized applications.
