Prism Central Deployment

  • While Prism Element runs on each Nutanix node, it is designed to only manage the local cluster which that node is a member of. Prism Central offers federated management of multiple clusters and provides more advanced analytics, user management, automation, and features. The following sections detail the implementation of Prism Central, including the prerequisites.

    Subnet creation

    Prior to Prism deployment, create a subnet where Prism will be deployed. A subnet is synonymous with a VM Network. Follow the steps below.

    1. Like the networking section earlier, navigate to Settings -> Network Configuration and select the Subnets tab on the right-hand side. Click on + Create Subnet.
    1. Enter a Subnet Name, select a Virtual Switch, and provide the tagged VLAN ID (use VLAN ID 0 for access ports). If you want AHV to control IPAM, click the box and then provide the network prefix and the gateway. The example below uses the VLAN ID of 105 which is the public network and does not enable IP management. Click Save.

    Figure 40.    Create subnet workflow

    1. Navigate to Settings -> Cluster Details. Provide an available IP address on the Host/CVM VLAN for the Data Services IP (DSIP) field. Click Save.

    Prism Central Deployment

    The following section includes the steps to deploy Prism Central from an existing Nutanix cluster. Refer to the Nutanix Prism Central Deployment Guide for more details.

    1. From the dashboard of Prism Element, find the Prism Central widget and select Register or create new.

    Figure 41.    Prism Central can be deployed from Prism Element

    1. In the initial dialogue shown in the following figure, select Deploy.

    Figure 42.    Deploy Prism Central instance workflow

    1. Select Upload Installation Binary. Select the appropriate .json and .tar file and click Upload. Once it is complete, the latest version will appear as in the Available versions table. Highlight the radio button and click Next.

    Figure 43.    Choose the Prism Central version to deploy

    1. In the PC Size and Scale screen decide how large to scale the Prism Central deployment. Note that X-Small is for exclusive use cases and should normally not be selected as it lacks support for some features. Click Next.

    Figure 44.    Choose the Prism Central size to deploy

    1. In the configuration page select the previously created network in the Subnets section. Provide the required network information, select the default Dell PowerFlex Container, provide a VM Name and IP Address.

    Figure 45.    Configure Prism Central networking details

    1. In the final step Nutanix presents the Microservices infrastructure. Dell recommends accepting the defaults.

    Figure 46.    Configure Prism Central Microservices

    Note: Prism Central Microservices configuration relies on a healthy and properly configured DNS Address in the previous step. An unexpected DNS server response can cause a failure in the Microservices step of the deployment workflow.

    1. A new Prism Central deployment will require an admin password change. It is recommended to perform this before cluster registration. One method is to open Prism Central by navigating to the following URL: https://<PRISM_CENTRAL_IP>:9440. Prism Central prompts for an admin password change at first login. Accept the EULA and enable Pulse if possible.

    Figure 47.    Prism Central UI with Pulse enable or disable feature

    Another method is to SSH into the Prism Central IP address and issue the following command:

    ncli user reset-password user-name="admin" password="<new password>"

    Note: The maximum age of the admin account password before a rotation is forced (default 60 days) can be configured via SSH into Prism Central with the following command:
    allssh sudo chage -M <MAX_DAYS> admin

    Previously used passwords are “remembered” in:
    /etc/security/opasswd

    A locked admin account can be unlocked with the following command:
    sudo faillock --user admin --reset

    1. Return to Prism Element. The cluster must be registered. Follow the registration link from the Prism Element dashboard.

    Figure 48.    Use Prism Element to register the cluster to Prism Central

    1. Click Connect.
    2. Provide the Prism Central connection information and click Connect.

    Prism Central is now deployed with the NCI-C cluster registered. Prism Central should be used going forward for most NCI-C tasks.

    Figure 49.    Prism Central Infrastructure dashboard

    Viewing Attached External Storage in Prism Central

    This section describes how to view the external storage in Prism Central. Use this procedure to view the external storage in Prism Central. To view the external storage (Dell PowerFlex storage clusters), follow these steps:

    1. Log on to Prism Central.
    1. From the Application Switcher Function, select the Infrastructure application, and from the navigation bar, select Hardware > External Storages. The External Storages tab provides the following information about the external storage:
      1. Name: Indicates the name of the attached External Storage. For example, PowerFlex.
      2. Unique ID: Indicates the unique identification of the external storage hardware.
      3. Status: Indicates the health status of the attached external storage. The values are:

    i             Healthy: Indicates the external storage object is healthy.

    ii           Authentication Failed: Indicates failure to log into the external storage due to incorrect credentials or credentials issue at the external storage (Dell PowerFlex storage cluster).

    iii         IO Error: Indicates the external storage object is unreachable for the IO or control operations due to network issues or if the external storage system is down.

    iv         Out of Space: Indicates the external storage is out of space.

    v           API Server Unavailable: Indicates the external storage API server is unavailable or unreachable due to network issues or if the external storage API server is down.

    1. Storage Vendor: Indicates the name of the external storage vendor. For example, Dell PowerFlex.
    2. Storage Usage: Indicates the storage usage and total capacity of the external storage.
    3. Storage Management: Provides access to the platform provided by the external storage vendor to manage storage. Click the Open link to access the platform. For example, Dell PowerFlex Manager if Dell PowerFlex is the external storage.
    4. Cluster: Indicates the name of the NCI-C cluster to which the selected Dell PowerFlex external storage is attached.

    The system displays the External Storages page with a List tab by default. This tab lists all the Dell PowerFlex external storages attached to the Dell PowerFlex NCI-C clusters that are registered to Prism Central.

Software and Firmware Life Cycle Management

  • This section describes how to manage the software and firmware upgrades for the NCI-C cluster and Dell PowerFlex storage cluster nodes.

    Software upgrade for the Nutanix compute cluster

    You can use the Nutanix LCM to update software on the compute nodes without downtime for the NCI-C cluster. For more information on upgrading the software for the NCI-C cluster, see Firmware and Software Updates Management.

    Firmware upgrade for the Dell PowerFlex compute servers in the Nutanix compute cluster

    This section describes how to perform the firmware upgrade for the Dell PowerFlex compute servers in the Nutanix compute cluster. Nutanix does not support Dell PowerFlex firmware upgrades through Life Cycle Manager (LCM). However, you can manually upgrade the firmware on Dell PowerFlex nodes in Nutanix Cloud Platform (NCP) compute cluster. To manually upgrade the firmware on Dell PowerFlex nodes in the Nutanix compute cluster, follow these steps:

    1. Before you start the firmware upgrade on any node, the node must be put in Maintenance Mode. For more information, see Putting a Node into Maintenance Mode using Web Console.
    1. After the host is successfully placed into maintenance mode, log on to the Dell PowerFlex Manager to begin the firmware upgrade on the node. For more information, see How to Use Dell PowerFlex Manager to Update Firmware on External Compute-only Nodes.

    Note: Make sure that the serial number of the node to be updated matches the one that is placed in maintenance mode.

    1. After the firmware upgrade is completed, exit the node from the maintenance mode. For more information, see Exiting a Node from the Maintenance Mode using Web Console.
    2. You must wait for the cluster to be healthy before upgrading to the next node.
    3. Follow the above steps for each node to upgrade in the cluster.

    Software and firmware upgrade for Dell PowerFlex storage cluster

    The Dell PowerFlex Manager independently manages the Dell PowerFlex storage cluster, including firmware and software updates. You cannot use Prism Central to manage the Dell PowerFlex storage cluster, but you can use Prism Central to manage the NCI-C cluster.

    For more information on how to upgrade the software and firmware for External Dell PowerFlex Storage Cluster, see Update firmware and software on Dell PowerFlex.

Storage Class

  • Using the Nutanix CSI driver, NKP clusters consume PowerFlex external storage for various roles such as pod ephemeral disks and persistent volumes. Consumption of storage is accomplished by using a storage class. The default storage class name in NKP is nutanix-volume.

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart ~]$ kubectl get storageclass

    NAME                       PROVISIONER       RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE      ALLOWVOLUMEEXPANSION   AGE

    nutanix-volume (default)   csi.nutanix.com   Delete          WaitForFirstConsumer   true                   3h4m

    Note: The volume binding mode for the nutanix-volume storage class is WaitForFirstConsumer (as opposed to Immediate). This means that a storage allocation will remain in a pending state and will not be consumed until the storage allocation becomes active in a scheduled pod.

    The nutanix-volume storage class is tied to the storage container specified at the time of the NKP cluster deployment. In the example below, the nutanix-volume storage class is tied to the pfxm.powerflex-tme.lab storage container.

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart ~]$ kubectl describe storageclass nutanix-volume

    Name:                  nutanix-volume

    IsDefaultClass:        Yes

    Annotations:           storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=true

    Provisioner:           csi.nutanix.com

    Parameters:            csi.storage.k8s.io/controller-expand-secret-name=nutanix-csi-credentials,csi.storage.k8s.io/controller-expand-secret-namespace=ntnx-system,csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype=ext4,csi.storage.k8s.io/node-publish-secret-name=nutanix-csi-credentials,csi.storage.k8s.io/node-publish-secret-namespace=ntnx-system,csi.storage.k8s.io/provisioner-secret-name=nutanix-csi-credentials,csi.storage.k8s.io/provisioner-secret-namespace=ntnx-system,description=CSI StorageClass nutanix-volume for nkp-workload,hypervisorAttached=ENABLED,storageContainer=pfxm.powerflex-tme.lab,storageType=NutanixVolumes

    AllowVolumeExpansion:  True

    MountOptions:          <none>

    ReclaimPolicy:         Delete

    VolumeBindingMode:     WaitForFirstConsumer

    Events:                <none>

Terminology

  • The following tables provide definitions for some of the terms that are used in this document, Dell PowerFlex concepts, and Nutanix Cloud Platform concepts.

    Table 1.      Dell PowerFlex terminology

    Term

    Definition

    D@RE

    Data at rest encryption.

    Device

    Local, direct attached block storage (DAS) in a node that is managed by an SDS and contributes to a storage pool.

    Fault Set

    A collection of SDSs that are managed together as a single fault unit. When employed, the distributed mesh-mirror copies of data are never placed within the same fault set.

    FG

    A “fine granularity” data layout on the storage disks comprising a storage pool. This storage pool option is designed for space efficiency, especially with heavy snapshot use. It requires the use of NVDIMMs or Software-Defined Persistent Memory (SDPM) modules and enables PowerFlex’s inline compression features.

    Intelligent Catalog (IC)

    A software bundle that contains operating system images and other software components used for deploying and managing PowerFlex nodes.

    MDM

    Metadata Manager. A highly available storage management cluster that resides alongside other software components within the system but sits outside the data path and supervises storage cluster health and configuration. It coordinates rebalancing and rebuilding/reprotecting data as changes occur in the system.

    MDS

    Management data store. The PowerFlex management data store is on the dedicated multi-node management controller used in PowerFlex rack systems. It is different from the data store used in a co-resident option. Kubernetes VMs host the management containers that reside on this data store.

    MG

    A “medium granularity” data layout on the storage disks comprising a storage pool. This is the original storage pool data layout option and provides very high performance.

    MVM

    Management virtual machine. The PowerFlex Manager UI is hosted in a Kubernetes environment running across a series of Linux machines. The VM version is called the management VM. The operating system is a customized SLES. version maintained by Dell Technologies.

    PFMC

    PowerFlex management controller. The infrastructure underlying the PowerFlex management platform in a dedicated multi-node configuration. It is mandatory in the PowerFlex rack, and optional for PowerFlex appliance. The physical controllers with VMware ESXi hosting PowerFlex management platform can be a three-node or a five-node VMware ESXi cluster with:

    • PowerFlex as shared storage (PowerFlex management controller 2.0)
    • vSan (PowerFlex management controller 1.0) Use in upgrades from PowerFlex 3.8.x systems only.

    PowerFlex management controller also hosts VMs for vCenter, a jump server, and other optional NSX or CloudLink managers.

    PFMP

    PowerFlex Management Platform. The management software stack for PowerFlex Manager runs on physical or virtual Linux instances, which are containers that provide services. This management solution can be implemented on various infrastructure options.

    Protection Domain

    A protection domain is a logical entity that consists of a group of SDSs that provide data protection for each other. Each SDS belongs to one (and only one) protection domain. Each protection domain is a unique set of SDSs. Protection domains can be added during installation and modified post-installation.

    Release Certification Matrix (RCM)

    A document outlining compatible hardware and software versions for Dell PowerFlex systems, ensuring smooth upgrades and deployments by providing a guide for IT professionals.

    RO

    Read Only

    RW

    Read Write

    SDC

    Storage Data Client. A client kernel driver that provides front-end volume access to operating systems, applications, or hypervisors. It presents PowerFlex volumes as local block devices. The SDC maintains peer-to-peer connections to every SDS managing a storage pool. It translates between the proprietary PowerFlex data transport protocol and block SCSI commands.

    SDR

    Storage Data Replicator. A software service that runs on PowerFlex Storage Nodes that manages storage data replication between pairs of PowerFlex systems.

    SDS

    Storage Data Server. A software service, running on a node that contributes disks to the storage cluster. Working together, several SDSs abstract local storage, maintain storage pools, and present volumes to the SDCs. Each SDS node is a fault unit, and the distributed mesh-mirror copies of data are never placed on the same fault unit.

    SDT

    Storage Data Target. Enables NVMe initiator clients to map and use PowerFlex volumes using the NVMe/TCP protocol. The SDT software service translates between the NVMe and proprietary PowerFlex protocols, supports discovery services, and manages client host connections.

    Storage Pool (PowerFlex)

    A storage pool is a set of physical storage devices within a protection domain. Each storage device belongs to one (and only one) storage pool. A volume is distributed over all devices residing in the same storage pool.

    System

    A PowerFlex system is the collection of entities managed by the Metadata Management (MDM) cluster.

    Volume

    Analogous to a LUN, a volume is a subset of a storage pool’s capacity presented by an SDC as a local block device. A volume’s data is evenly distributed across all disks comprising a storage pool, according to the data layout selected for that storage pool.

    Table 2.      Nutanix Cloud Platform terminology

    Term

    Definition

    aCLI

    The AOS command-line interface.

    Acropolis

    Nutanix converged software fabric for virtualization and storage management. It comprises AOS, Nutanix storage, AHV, Prism, and Acropolis APIs.

    ADFS

    Advanced Disc Filing System

    Advertised Capacity

    The maximum storage size that a container can use. The advertised capacity of the container is the value defined by the admin multiplied by the replication factor.

    AHV

    Acropolis Hypervisor. A KVM-based virtualization platform that powers VMs and containers for applications and cloud-native workloads on-premises and in public clouds.

    AOS

    The Acropolis operating system or base software that is installed as a Controller Virtual Machine (CVM) atop a hypervisor to manage everything in a Nutanix cluster. (Formerly NOS.)

    Cassandra

    A distributed, high-performance, scalable database that collects all metadata about the guest VM data stored in a Nutanix datastore.

    Cerebro

    Coordinates all disaster recovery replication activities between clusters for Protection Domain (PD)-based-DR and deals with snapshots.

    Chronos

    A job and task scheduler.

    Cluster CLI

    CLI is used in the CVM to manage a Nutanix cluster. Create, destroy, status, start, stop.

    Consistency Group (Nutanix)

    A subset of VMs in a protection domain. All VMs within a consistency group for that protection domain are snapshotted with a single snapshot in a crash-consistent manner.

    Controller VM (CVM)

    A Nutanix VM that manages storage and other cluster functions on a node. A controller VM is also known as a Service VM (SVM). (Formerly SVM.)

    Curator

    A service that maintains the overall health of clusters and the file system, performs garbage collection, and maintains the consistency of metadata.

    Data Resiliency

    A measure of the types of failures a cluster can withstand, affected by block awareness and redundancy factor.

    Degraded Node

    A node that contains a CVM that is in a partially unresponsive state and cannot reliably perform cluster operations at the same performance level as normal clusters.

    Disaster Recovery

    A process for migrating data to a remote site.

    Distributed Storage Fabric (DSF)

    Automatically tiers data across the cluster to different classes of storage devices using intelligent data placement algorithms. The algorithm ensures the most frequently used data is available in memory or in flash on the node local to the VM. Does not apply to external storage.

    DNS

    Domain Name System.

    Dynamic Ring Changer (DRC)

    Enables the addition, removal, and replacement of Cassandra nodes in a running cluster.

    Dynamic Scheduling (ADS)

    Proactively monitors your cluster for any compute and storage I/O contentions or hotspots over a period of time. If ADS detects a problem, ADS creates a migration plan that eliminates hotspots in the cluster by migrating VMs from one host to another.

    eCLI

    The Ergon command-line interface.

    Ergon

    A task management service.

    Flow Network Security

    An application-centric micro segmentation solution that provides protection of east-west traffic to your Nutanix environments based on stateful, distributed firewall policies. (Formerly Flow Micro segmentation.)

    Flow Virtual Networking

    Provides rich software-defined networking with multi-tenant isolation, self-service provisioning, and IP address preservation.

    Foundation

    A node imaging tool.

    Foundation Central

    A Nutanix service used to create clusters from factory-imaged nodes remotely from Prism Central.

    Frodo

    An AHV service that provides high-performance virtual disk I/O to the VMs.

    Genesis

    A service that runs on each node and manages cluster components and other services and is responsible for the initial configuration and service interactions, such as start and stop.

    Hades

    A disk management service that runs on Prism Element.

    HCI

    Hyper-Converged Infrastructure. The traditional Nutanix architectural model, combining compute, storage, and networking in each Nutanix cluster.

    Host

    An instance of the hypervisor that runs on a Nutanix node.

    Image Service

    A workflow in the Prism web console that lets you upload ISO or disk images (in ESXi or Hyper-V format) to a Nutanix AHV cluster by specifying a remote repository URL or by uploading a file from a local machine.

    IPAM

    IP Address Management.

    Kanon

    A policy enforcement engine that runs in Prism Central.

    KVM

    Kernel-based Virtual Machine.

    Lazan

    An advanced VM scheduler that provides VM scheduling plans and functions for AHV clusters.

    Live Migration

    A method of non-disruptively moving a guest VM from one AHV host to another AHV host or cluster while the VM is turned on, provided the target has available resources.

    Medusa

    The metadata store for the Nutanix distributed storage fabric

    Move

    A migration service for VMs and DBs. (Formerly Xtract.)

    Move Agent

    An agent service that is exclusive to Hyper-V migrations and is deployed on the Hyper-V host. The Move Agent communicates with the Source Agent and interfaces with the source VMs on the Hyper-V host to facilitate the migration.

    Move CLI

    Move command-line interface

    NCI

    Nutanix Cloud Infrastructure

    NCI-C

    Nutanix Cloud Infrastructure Compute

    nCLI

    The Nutanix command-line interface.

    NCP

    Nutanix Cloud Platform

    Network Controller

    A networking component of Prism Central that manages and controls configuration, monitoring, and optimization of network resources for Flow Virtual Networking. It provides programmability, automation, and centralized control for configuring and managing network flows. (Formerly Atlas Network Controller, Advanced Network Controller, ANC.)

    Node IP Address

    A collective term for the CVM and hypervisor IP addresses.

    NTP

    Network Time Protocol.

    Nutanix Block

    A rack-mountable enclosure that contains one to four Nutanix nodes. In multinode blocks, nodes only share the power supplies and fans.

    Nutanix Cluster

    A group of nodes contained in one or more Nutanix blocks.

    Nutanix Cluster Checker (NCC)

    Checks the health and alerts of a cluster and runs the log_collector.

    Nutanix Guest Agent

    Maintains a communication channel between the Controller VM (CVM) and the guest VMs.

    Nutanix Guest Tools (NGT)

    A software package with advanced VM management features that comes pre-installed with AOS.

    Nutanix Node

    A Nutanix server within a Nutanix Cluster which hosts virtual machines (VMs) and runs the Nutanix software stack, including AOS, AHV, and CVM.

    Nutanix Rack

    Both a physical and logical fault tolerance construct which contains one or more Nutanix Blocks.

    Nutanix Security Advisories

    Provides detailed information on the available security fixes and updates, including the vulnerability description and affected product or version.

    Nutanix Unified Storage NUS

    A software-defined data services platform, which includes Files, Objects, Volumes, and Data Lens, that simplifies enterprise data storage operations.

    Open vSwitch (OVS)

    An open-source software switch implemented in the Linux kernel and designed to work in a multiserver virtualization environment. By default, OVS behaves like a layer 2 learning switch that maintains a MAC address table. The hypervisor host and VMs connect to virtual ports on the switch.

    Pithos

    vDisk configuration manager. Responsible for vDisk configuration data. Runs on every node and is built on top of Cassandra.

    Prism

    A single web-based networking, infrastructure, and operations management interface for Nutanix clusters.

    Prism Central

    A centralized management tool that runs as a separate VM to monitor and manage multiple clusters through a single web console.

    Prism Element

    A web console for managing a single Nutanix cluster.

    Pulse

    Prism's health monitoring system provides diagnostic system data to Nutanix Support to deliver proactive, context-aware support for Nutanix solutions. Pulse unobtrusively collects this information with no effect on system performance. Pulse shares only basic system-level information necessary for monitoring the health and status of a Nutanix cluster.

    Redundancy Factor

    The number of nodes, plus one, that the cluster can tolerate being down at one time. By default, Nutanix clusters have a redundancy factor of two, which means that they can tolerate one node being down. They are configurable to redundancy factor three to enable tolerating two nodes being down. (Formerly RF.)

    Replication Factor

    The number of copies of data kept by a container. The default is two. Containers on clusters with a redundancy factor of three can have a replication factor of three. (Formerly RF.)

    Reserved Capacity

    A property of a container or vDisk that guarantees that a certain amount of storage space is available.

    Scheduler (ADS)

    A service that proactively monitors your cluster for any compute or storage I/O contention or hotspots over a period of time.

    Self-Service Container

    A storage container created on the target cluster and used by Prism Self Service for storage and other feature operations.

    Self-Service Restore

    Allows a user to restore a file within a virtual machine from the Nutanix protected snapshot with minimal Nutanix administrator intervention.

    Shadow Clones

    A cache of a vDisk on all the nodes in the cluster. When a vDisk is read by multiple VMs (such as the base image for a VDI clone pool), the cluster creates shadow clones of the vDisk.

    Stargate

    A core service that implements most of the functionality in the distributed storage fabric. Stargate is the primary process responsible for reading and writing information to disks in the cluster

    Storage Container

    A subset of available storage within a storage pool. Data written to a vDisk ends up on the hardware resources contained within that container. Multiple containers can own the same hardware.

    Storage Pool (Nutanix)

    A group of physical disks from one or more tiers.

    Thin Provisioning

    A mechanism that permits dynamic provisioning of space for a vDisk. Thin provisioning allocates space on demand.

    Uhura

    A virtualization management service.

    vDisk

    Data associated with a VM represented as a set of files on a datastore. Each vDisk is associated with a unique container. Each vDisk corresponds to one or more volumes on PowerFlex external storage.

    VLAN

    Virtual Local Area Network. A logical grouping of network devices that allows segmentation of network traffic and isolates devices on a single physical network, improving security and network management.

    VM

    Virtual Machine

    Volume Group (Nutanix)

    A collection of logically related virtual disks. Block storage grouping, backed by volumes (LUNs) and exposed up as one or multiple iSCSI targets.

    X-Ray

    A tool that performs tests that intentionally create infrastructure load or node-failure situations to replicate real-world activity within the datacenter.

    Zeus

    A service that holds configuration details and works closely with Zookeeper.

    Zookeeper

    A centralized service for maintaining configuration information, naming, providing distributed synchronization, and providing group service.

Volumes

  • Nutanix consumes external storage through the creation of volumes on PowerFlex. Nutanix virtual disks, or vDisks, can be attached to virtual machines directly using Prism Central, or through the use of volume groups. Volume groups allow the mapping of volumes as virtual disks through iSCSI and the cluster Data Services IP (DSIP).

    From a management perspective, most PowerFlex volumes are equal in that they can be created, mapped, expanded in size, replicated, unmapped, and deleted using the PowerFlex Manager UI and workflows. However,  PowerFlex Manager 4.6.2 introduced a new ‘ntnx’ volume class for Nutanix volumes. The volume class enables the use of the Filter Volume feature in PowerFlex Manager to toggle the display of Nutanix volumes as either shown or hidden. All Nutanix volumes created on the Dell PowerFlex are prefixed with “nx_” as shown in the figure below. The volume name extension or suffix identifies the type of volume:

    • .nd – per-node volumes. These are AOS metadata volumes and the first volumes created by an NCI-C cluster when external storage is added. These volumes are mapped and formatted as ext4 and mounted under /home/nutanix/data/stargate-storage/disks/. In addition, these volumes are placed in zeus_config in external_storage_disk_list with the volume id, size, mount path. Verbose information about these volumes can be obtained with the zeus_config_printer command in the CVM.

      Three per-node volumes per CVM are created initially:
    • One 8GB for Cassandra (metadata service). Additional volumes will be dynamically created and mounted if Cassandra volume exceeds a configurable threshold.
    • One 56GB for Curator (janitor service). Additional volumes will be dynamically created and mounted if Curator volume exceeds a configurable threshold.
    • One 8GB for Zookeeper (configuration information service)
    • Additional volumes per CVM are created for swap.
    • .dt – data volumes which correspond to a vDisk. These are sized according to the vDisk configuration in Prism but must adhere to the Dell PowerFlex sizing rules of the power of 8. For example, if a VM is configured with a 100 GB vDisk, the corresponding volume size in PowerFlex will be 104 GB.
    • Snapshots result in the creation of 1 additional RW snapshot volume. (net creation of 1 new PowerFlex volume)
    • A clone of a powered off VM results in the creation of 1 additional RW snapshot and 1 additional metadata volume (net creation of 2 new PowerFlex volumes).
    • A clone of a powered on VM results in the creation of 1 RO snapshot, 1 RW snapshot, and 1 metadata volume (net creation of 3 new PowerFlex volumes).
    • .md – metadata volumes. A thin provisioned 8 GB metadata volume is created for every data volume that is created. Nutanix uses these volumes for changed block tracking (CBT) and to store data-related information. Most of the time, these volumes are unmapped but Nutanix will map them when it needs to record data. For example, a volume under heavy activity or one involved in snapshots would prompt mapping. That mapping will be removed after idle time to avoid exceeding the SDC limit per node. Each vDisk clone will create an additional metadata volume. However, snapshots within a volume tree (vTree) share a single metadata volume. The per-volume vTree limit is 126. This is the maximum number of volumes allowed within a single vTree.

    Figure 50.    PowerFlex Manager block volumes of the type Nutanix

    Note: All day-to-day Nutanix volume management should be orchestrated by following standard Nutanix workflows in Prism. In most circumstances, Nutanix volumes should not be altered within PowerFlex Manager. To maintain integrity of the NCI-C cluster and its workloads, Nutanix volumes are natively protected by the ‘ntnx’ volume classification and cannot be deleted using PowerFlex Manager. However, Nutanix volumes can be queried, unmapped, and deleted forcefully using PowerFlex scli. As an example:
    scli --query_all_volumes
    scli --unmap_volume_from_host --volume_name <nx_xxx=yyy.dt> --volume_class ntnx
    scli --remove_volume --volume_name <nx_xxx=yyy.dt> --volume_class ntnx

Volumes

  • Using the nutanix-volume storage class, NKP clusters consume PowerFlex external storage similar to how virtual machine vDisks do. A storage allocation is backed by a thin provisioned data volume which equals the size of the storage allocation, in 8GB increments, as well as a thin provisioned 8GB metadata volume.

    Consider the following .yaml. When deployed, it instantiates a 992GB persistent volume claim and then a scheduled nginx pod consumes it:

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart demo-applications]$ cat task-pvc.yaml

    apiVersion: v1

    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim

    metadata:

      name: task-pv-claim

    spec:

      storageClassName: nutanix-volume

      accessModes:

        - ReadWriteOnce

      resources:

        requests:

          storage: 992Gi

    ---

    apiVersion: v1

    kind: Pod

    metadata:

      name: task-pv-pod

    spec:

      volumes:

        - name: task-pv-storage

          persistentVolumeClaim:

            claimName: task-pv-claim

      containers:

        - name: task-pv-container

          image: nginx

          ports:

            - containerPort: 80

              name: "http-server"

          volumeMounts:

            - mountPath: "/usr/share/nginx/html"

              name: task-pv-storage

    The pod is deployed in the jgbdemo namespace and the status of the persistent volume claim and the persistent volume is requested. Because the persistent volume claim was consumed in a scheduled pod, its status is Bound (instead of pending):

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart demo-applications]$ kubectl apply -f task-pvc.yaml -n jgbdemo

    persistentvolumeclaim/task-pv-claim created

    pod/task-pv-pod created

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart demo-applications]$ kubectl get pvc -n jgbdemo

    NAME            STATUS   VOLUME                                     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS     VOLUMEATTRIBUTESCLASS   AGE

    task-pv-claim   Bound    pvc-790b3ae3-299c-47e1-84cf-52294c940ee8   992Gi      RWO            nutanix-volume   <unset>                 12s

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart demo-applications]$ kubectl get pv -n jgbdemo

    NAME                                       CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM                   STORAGECLASS     VOLUMEATTRIBUTESCLASS   REASON   AGE

    pvc-790b3ae3-299c-47e1-84cf-52294c940ee8   992Gi      RWO            Delete           Bound    jgbdemo/task-pv-claim   nutanix-volume   <unset>                          3m25s

    Persistent volumes can be viewed in Prism Central under Compute | Kubernetes Clusters | Storage. From there, persistent volume capacity utilization, performance metrics, and other details can be viewed.

    Figure 71.    A persistent volume as seen in Prism Central

    Lastly, because the persistent volume claim is Bound, its backing data volume (and metadata volume) can be observed in PowerFlex Manager.

    Figure 72.    NKP persistent volume observed in PowerFlex Manager

    Just as with virtual machines and vDisks, the lifecycle of cloud native storage on PowerFlex is handled autonomously and seamlessly by NKP. While there is observability of storage consumption in PowerFlex Manager, the management of the volumes is delegated to NKP.

    This last application example will consume ephemeral storage and make use of the MetalLB load balancer in NKP across a replica set of three (3).

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart demo-applications]$ cat demo-hellokubernetes.yaml

    apiVersion: v1

    kind: Service

    metadata:

      name: hello-kubernetes

    spec:

      type: LoadBalancer

      ports:

      - port: 80

        targetPort: 8080

      selector:

        app: hello-kubernetes

    ---

    apiVersion: apps/v1

    kind: Deployment

    metadata:

      name: hello-kubernetes

    spec:

      replicas: 3

      selector:

        matchLabels:

          app: hello-kubernetes

      template:

        metadata:

          labels:

            app: hello-kubernetes

        spec:

          containers:

          - name: hello-kubernetes

            image: paulbouwer/hello-kubernetes:1.5

            imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent

            ports:

            - containerPort: 8080

    The application is deployed:

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart demo-applications]$ kubectl apply -f demo-hellokubernetes.yaml -n jgbdemo

    service/hello-kubernetes created

    deployment.apps/hello-kubernetes created

    After the application is deployed, view the replicasets, pods, and load balancer service external IP address:

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart demo-applications]$ kubectl get replicasets -n jgbdemo

    NAME                          DESIRED   CURRENT   READY   AGE

    hello-kubernetes-66647d4b59   3         3         3       9m

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart demo-applications]$ kubectl get pods -n jgbdemo

    NAME                                READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE

    hello-kubernetes-66647d4b59-drd2m   1/1     Running   0          9m6s

    hello-kubernetes-66647d4b59-sqv7n   1/1     Running   0          9m6s

    hello-kubernetes-66647d4b59-tfmtv   1/1     Running   0          9m6s

    task-pv-pod                         1/1     Running   0          19h

    [nutanix@nkp-quickstart demo-applications]$ kubectl get service -n jgbdemo

    NAME               TYPE           CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP     PORT(S)        AGE

    hello-kubernetes   LoadBalancer   10.109.39.191   172.105.16.57   80:32258/TCP   9m8s

    Lastly, the application front end can be accessed by a web browser using the external IP address:

    Figure 73.    The hello-kubernetes application front end accessed by a web browser
